group.title: Law and ethics
group.tagline: Rights, duties and right and wrong
sources: Words and CEFR levels chosen by the authors from general knowledge of English; meanings, examples and sentences are original

Word-list licences checked 2026-10-25: CEFR-J Wordlist 1.5 (Tono Laboratory, TUFS; free with citation, A1-B2) and NGSL/NAWL (CC BY-SA 4.0) were not copied; Oxford 3000 and English Vocabulary Profile terms were not confirmed, so they were not used

words.meaning: A small gap in a law that lets people avoid it legally.
examples: The company used a tax {loophole} to pay less.
wrong: A loophole is a rule that closes every gap in a law.

words.meaning: To change the law so that something is no longer a crime.
examples: Some countries have {decriminalized} jaywalking.
wrong: They decriminalized the act by making it a serious crime.

words.meaning: Basic freedoms, such as free speech, that the state must protect.
examples: Critics say the new spy law threatens {civil liberties}.
wrong: Civil liberties are rules that let the state silence anyone it likes.

words.meaning: A statement in court saying whether you are guilty or not.
examples: She entered a {plea} of not guilty.
wrong: The plea was the judge’s final sentence.

words.meaning: Said to be true or to have happened, but not yet proved.
examples: The {alleged} thief has not been charged yet.
wrong: The alleged crime was proved beyond all doubt in court.

words.meaning: The duty to show that a claim is true, especially in court.
examples: In a criminal trial, the {burden of proof} lies with the state.
wrong: The burden of proof means the accused must prove nothing ever happened.

words.meaning: The fair legal steps the state must follow before punishing anyone.
examples: Everyone has the right to {due process} under the law.
wrong: Due process allows the police to punish people without a trial.

words.meaning: The idea that everyone, including leaders, must obey the same laws.
examples: Democracy depends on the {rule of law}.
wrong: The rule of law means leaders can ignore any law they dislike.

words.meaning: A hard choice between two options that both seem right or wrong.
examples: Lying to protect a friend is a classic {moral dilemma}.
wrong: It was a moral dilemma because the right choice was totally obvious.

words.meaning: Not morally acceptable, especially in work or business.
examples: Testing on people without telling them is {unethical}.
wrong: Her unethical behavior earned her a prize for honesty.

words.meaning: The inner sense that tells you whether what you do is right or wrong.
examples: His {conscience} would not let him keep the money.
wrong: With a clear conscience, he felt terribly guilty.

words.meaning: The crime of giving money or gifts to make someone act dishonestly.
examples: The official was jailed for {bribery}.
wrong: Bribery is paying your taxes on time.

words.meaning: A person who helps someone else commit a crime.
examples: The robber’s {accomplice} waited in the car.
wrong: His accomplice tried to stop the robbery and called the police.

words.meaning: A person who reveals wrongdoing inside an organization.
examples: A {whistleblower} told reporters about the hidden safety reports.
wrong: The whistleblower helped the firm keep its crimes secret.

words.meaning: The duty to keep private information secret.
examples: Doctors must respect patient {confidentiality}.
wrong: Confidentiality means sharing private details with everyone.

words.meaning: Permission to do something, freely given.
examples: You cannot use her photo without her {consent}.
wrong: He gave his consent by clearly refusing.

words.meaning: A person’s inner sense of what is right and wrong, used to guide choices.
examples: Her strong {moral compass} kept her honest under pressure.
wrong: With no moral compass, he always knew the right thing to do.

words.meaning: To make new laws.
examples: Parliament plans to {legislate} against online scams.
wrong: The judge legislated by applying an old law to one case.

words.meaning: To support or keep a law, decision or principle.
examples: The court {upheld} the original ruling.
wrong: Judges uphold the law by ignoring it completely.

words.meaning: To break a law or limit someone’s rights.
examples: The new rule may {infringe} on free speech.
wrong: The law infringes on our rights by protecting them fully.

words.meaning: To break a law, rule or agreement.
examples: The company {violated} safety rules.
wrong: He violated the contract by doing exactly what it said.

words.meaning: Having a good reason, so it can be accepted as right.
examples: Self-defense can be a {justifiable} reason for using force.
wrong: His justifiable anger had no reason behind it at all.

words.meaning: Allowed by the law.
examples: Peaceful protest is {lawful} in most countries.
wrong: Stealing a car is a lawful activity.

words.meaning: Not allowed by law or by accepted rules.
examples: Police found {illicit} drugs in the van.
wrong: The illicit trade was fully approved by the government.

words.meaning: The lawyers who try to prove in court that someone is guilty.
examples: The {prosecution} called its first witness.
wrong: The prosecution argued that the accused was innocent.

words.meaning: The police and other groups whose job is to make people obey laws.
examples: Local {law enforcement} closed the road after the crash.
wrong: Law enforcement is the group that helps criminals escape.

words.meaning: The process of taking a dispute to court.
examples: The two firms are locked in costly {litigation}.
wrong: They avoided litigation by suing each other in court.

words.meaning: Not allowed to be used as evidence in court.
examples: The recording was ruled {inadmissible} by the judge.
wrong: The inadmissible evidence was the main proof shown to the jury.

words.meaning: The crime of lying in court after promising to tell the truth.
examples: The witness was charged with {perjury}.
wrong: Perjury is telling the full truth in court.

words.meaning: A false spoken statement that harms someone’s reputation.
examples: He sued his neighbor for {slander}.
wrong: Her slander praised him and told only the truth.

words.meaning: A right to have or receive something.
examples: Paid leave is a legal {entitlement} for workers.
wrong: An entitlement is something you have no right to.

words.meaning: Moral beliefs that stop you from doing something wrong.
examples: A man with no {scruples} will lie to anyone.
wrong: Her scruples made her happy to cheat her friends.

words.meaning: A good moral quality in a person.
examples: Patience is a {virtue}.
wrong: Cruelty is one of her finest virtues.

words.meaning: Saying you have beliefs that you do not follow yourself.
examples: It’s {hypocrisy} to preach saving water and fill a pool every day.
wrong: His hypocrisy showed in how closely he followed his own advice.

words.meaning: A rule applied unfairly, more strictly to some people than to others.
examples: Punishing girls but not boys for the same thing is a {double standard}.
wrong: A double standard means everyone is judged by exactly the same rule.

words.meaning: The benefit of most people, even if a few lose out.
examples: She gave up her bonus for {the greater good} of the team.
wrong: He acted for the greater good by helping only himself.

words.meaning: Not having to obey the laws that apply to everyone else.
examples: No one, not even a president, is {above the law}.
wrong: He thinks he is above the law, so he obeys every rule carefully.

words.meaning: Responsible for something wrong and deserving blame.
examples: The court found the driver {culpable} for the crash.
wrong: She was culpable, so she was not to blame at all.

words.meaning: Bad or dishonest behavior by someone in a position of trust.
examples: The officer was fired for serious {misconduct}.
wrong: He got a promotion for his professional misconduct.

words.meaning: Careless or wrong work by a professional, such as a doctor or lawyer.
examples: The surgeon was sued for {malpractice} after the failed operation.
wrong: Malpractice is the careful, correct work of a skilled professional.
